When Sharks Attack: An analysis and visualization of trends in shark attack reports¶

I am a lover of all things sharks. Unfortunately, there is an abundance of misinformation about sharks and their behaviour, often creating the impression that sharks viciously hunt and attack humans. However, considering the circumstances under which shark attacks occur can help us mitigate risks and understand that attacks are both rare and not related to predation on humans. I am choosing to explore a data set recording logistical and forensic information from a collection of shark attacks occurring worldwide over a period of more than one hundred years. By analyzing the information in this data set, I am hoping to determine which conditions appear to be associated with increased incidence or risk of shark attacks.

The data set I am using for this project can be accessed through this link: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/felipeesc/shark-attack-dataset/data

Questions of interest¶

  • Are there any geographical patterns in the incidence of shark attacks?
  • What water activities are most associated with shark attacks?
  • Are there any species of sharks that can be identified as more likely to attack than others?

Sorting out the 'Species' Column¶

At this point in the data wrangling process, there are 1549 entry types in the species column. For example, attacks involving tiger sharks have been listed as 'Tiger shark', '2 m tiger shark', '3 m tiger shark', etc., though all these observations should be listed as 'Tiger Shark' for the purpose of data analysis. I reviewed the data to determine the different categories of shark species present, and wrote functions to replace entries containing relevant keywords with standard category names. Many of the entries had no species information, and included only information pertaining to the size of the shark, such as 'large', 'small', '0.9-2 m', etc. In these cases, I considered the species 'Unknown'.

In [4]:
def replace_tiger(dataframe, column):
    mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('tiger', case = False)
    dataframe.loc[mask, column] = 'Tiger Shark'
    return dataframe
 

def replace_white(dataframe, column):
    mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('white', case = False)
    dataframe.loc[mask, column] = 'Great White Shark'
    return dataframe

def replace_unknown_digits(dataframe, column):
    mask = dataframe[column].str.contains(r"\d", case = False)

def replace_unknown_other(dataframe, column, species):
    mask = ~dataframe[column].str.contains('|'.join(species), case = False)
    dataframe.loc[mask, column] = 'Unknown'
    return dataframe

Which Shark Species are Most Likely to Attack?¶

Even though the data has been cleaned and sorted, in most attacks the species of shark involved was unknown. As we can see from a preliminary plot, most of the cases where the species was known are obscured by the cases where it was not.

In [5]:
#Preliminary plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize = (30, 5))
sns.histplot(data = attacks_df, x = 'Species ')
plt.xticks(rotation = 90)
plt.show()

What can be done?¶

In an attempt to analyze the data and draw some conclusions, I will perform bootstrap sampling on the data where the species of shark was known, to get an idea of which species of sharks may be more likely to be involved in an attack.

Reflecting on the data¶

Based on the bootstrap distribution, we might infer that Great White sharks (mean proportion = 0.39), Tiger sharks (mean proportion = 0.17), and Bull sharks (mean proportion = 0.10) are most likely to be involved in shark attacks, with Great White sharks representing a strong majority. This observation is consistent with shark attack literature; these trends may be associated with their vast distribution worldwide and subsequent greater likelihood to be in contact with humans (Midway et al., 2019).

Geographical Patterns in Shark Attacks¶

Based on a preliminary plot, there are a number of countries with much greater contributions to the number of worldwide shark attacks than others. To simplify this analysis, I will focus on the ten countries with the greatest number of attacks in the dataset.

Already, we can see that the USA is strongly influencing the average number of shark attacks globally, bringing the average number of attacks even about the boundaries of the interquartile range. Further analysis of the most affected countries can further reveal geographical trends.

Reflecting on the data¶

By further decomposing the number of attacks in each country by area, we can see which regions have the strongest influences on the trends in their respective country. We can see, for example, that states in the southern USA are the primary contributors to USA shark attacks, which is logical given their proximity to warm coastal waters where shark activity in shallow waters is greater (Neff & Hueter, 2013).

What Activities have the Potential to Increase Risk of Shark Attacks?¶

Much like the species data, there are a staggering number of entry types for the activity the victims were participating in at the time of the attacks. A preliminary plot shows that this data is currently not very useful for analysis and should be processed in a similar way to the species data in order to be meaningful.

Sorting out the 'Activity' column¶

Note that for entries involving fishing and/or boating, I sorted the data into 'Fishing', 'Boating', 'Fishing from a boat', and 'Shipwreck' categories within one function to avoid miscategorizing the data, as many relevant keywords overlapped between these categories.

In [16]:
def replace_swim(dataframe, column):
    mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('swim', case = False)
    dataframe.loc[mask, column] = 'Swimming'
    return dataframe
 
def replace_surf(dataframe, column):
    mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('surf', case = False)
    dataframe.loc[mask, column] = 'Surfing'
    return dataframe

def replace_board(dataframe, column):
    mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('board', case = False)
    dataframe.loc[mask, column] = 'Surfing'
    return dataframe

def replace_bath(dataframe, column):
    mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('bath', case = False)
    dataframe.loc[mask, column] = 'Bathing'
    return dataframe
    
def replace_dive(dataframe, column):
    mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('div', case = False)
    dataframe.loc[mask, column] = 'Diving'
    return dataframe

def replace_lasso(dataframe, column):
    mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('lasso', case = False)
    dataframe.loc[mask, column] = 'Attempting to lasso/catch the shark'
    return dataframe

def replace_rescue(dataframe, column):
    mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('rescue', case = False)
    dataframe.loc[mask, column] = 'Rescue'
    return dataframe

def replace_collect(dataframe, column):
    mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('collect', case = False)
    dataframe.loc[mask, column] = 'Collecting shells or other marine objects'
    return dataframe

def replace_crossing(dataframe, column):
    mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('cross', case = False)
    dataframe.loc[mask, column] = 'Crossing a body of water'
    return dataframe

def replace_provoke(dataframe, column):
    free_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('free', case = False)
    chase_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('chase', case = False)
    catch_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('catch', case = False)
    hook_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('hook', case = False)
    fists_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('fists', case = False)
    drive_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('drive', case = False)
    kill_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('kill', case = False)
    ride_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('ride', case = False)
    net_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('net', case = False)
    dataframe.loc[free_mask | chase_mask | catch_mask | hook_mask | fists_mask | drive_mask | kill_mask
    | ride_mask | net_mask] = 'Provoked/Chose to interact with shark'
    return dataframe
    
def replace_fish_and_boat(dataframe, column): 
    fish_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('fish', case = False)
    boat_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('boat', case = False)
    shipwreck_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('sink', case = False)
    shipwreck_mask_2 = dataframe[column].str.contains('sank', case = False)
    shipwreck_mask_3 = dataframe[column].str.contains('sunk', case = False)
    overboard_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('overboard', case = False)
    adrift_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('adrift', case = False)
    abandon_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('abandon', case = False)
    capsize_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('capsize', case = False)
    raft_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('raft', case = False)
    plane_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('plane', case = False)
    plane_mask_2 = dataframe[column].str.contains('air', case = False)
    accident_mask = dataframe[column].str.contains('accident', case = False)
    dataframe.loc[fish_mask & boat_mask & ~shipwreck_mask & ~shipwreck_mask_2 & ~shipwreck_mask_3
    & ~overboard_mask & ~adrift_mask & ~abandon_mask & ~capsize_mask & ~raft_mask & ~plane_mask & ~plane_mask_2
    & ~accident_mask, column] = 'Fishing from a Boat'
    dataframe.loc[fish_mask & ~boat_mask, column] = 'Fishing'
    dataframe.loc[boat_mask & ~fish_mask & ~shipwreck_mask & ~shipwreck_mask_2 & ~shipwreck_mask_3
    & ~overboard_mask & ~adrift_mask & ~abandon_mask & ~capsize_mask & ~raft_mask & ~plane_mask & ~plane_mask_2
    & ~accident_mask, column] = 'Boating'
    dataframe.loc[shipwreck_mask | shipwreck_mask_2 | shipwreck_mask_3| overboard_mask | adrift_mask | abandon_mask
    | capsize_mask | raft_mask | plane_mask | plane_mask_2 | accident_mask ] = 'Shipwreck or Plane Crash' 
    return dataframe

def replace_other(dataframe, column, activity):
    mask = ~dataframe[column].str.contains('|'.join(activity), case = False)
    dataframe.loc[mask, column] = 'Other'
    return dataframe

attacks_df = replace_dive(attacks_df, 'Activity')
attacks_df = replace_lasso(attacks_df, 'Activity')

Reflecting on the data¶

Surfing (mean proportion = 0.32), fishing (mean proportion = 0.24), and swimming (mean proportion = 0.24) appear to be the most common activities associated with shark attacks. Surfing may have the highest rates due to its association with a greater number of hours spent in the water, in comparison to diving (mean proportion = 0.11), for example, where time in the water is limited by the constraints of equipment (ex. air supply).

General Conclusions¶

From the above analyses, we might infer that risk of shark attacks is mainly a question of proximity; under which conditions are humans most likely to be in close contact with a shark? We can see that the sharks most likely to attack are also the most numerous, and that attacks are more likely to occur in regions that sharks frequent, while engaging in activities that prolong time in the water. Like many animals, sharks are curious and may choose to investigate a novel feature of their environment (i.e. a human in the water). This is not equivalent to predation, and though encounters with sharks can be dangerous or even (very rarely) deadly, they are not usually malicious (Neff & Hueter, 2013).

Limitations¶

The categorical nature of this data limited the number of descriptive statistics that could be calculated, so analyses were focused on the frequencies and proportions of values and visualized accordingly.

To get some insight on the possible reasons for these shark attack trends, I consulted the following journal articles:
